M4.rect-squares.09.text: A square with a side of {a|square|squares|squares} is made bigger: its side becomes one square longer. By how many squares does the area grow?

The old area is {a} × {a} = {=a*a}. Work out the area of the new square, {=a+1} by {=a+1}, and take the old area away.

M4.rect-squares.10.text: One square is cut out of the corner of a rectangle that is {a} by {b|square|squares|squares}. The side of one square is {=1} cm. Find the perimeter of the figure that is left, in centimetres.

So the perimeter stays the same as that of the whole rectangle: ({a} + {b}) × {=2} = {=2*(a+b)}.

Two sides of the cut-out square were on the border and two other sides are now on it. Does the perimeter of the {a} by {b} rectangle change?

M4.rect-squares.11.text: A staircase is made of squares: the bottom row has {a|square|squares|squares}, the row above has one square fewer, and so on up to one square at the top. The side of one square is {=1} cm. Find the perimeter of the staircase in centimetres.

The stepped side: all its horizontal parts together make {a} cm and all its vertical parts together make {a} cm.

So the outline is as long as that of a square with a side of {a} cm. How many sides does it have?

explain.area: {w_area} is the number of squares. The question is about the perimeter.

M4.rect-sides.01.text: The sides of a rectangle are {a} cm and {b} cm. Find its perimeter.

The perimeter has this pair twice, so we double it.

M4.rect-sides.02.text: The sides of a rectangle are {a} cm and {b} cm. Find its area.

One row holds {a} squares and there are {b} rows.
Altogether {a} × {b} = {r}, so the area is {r} cm².

One row holds {a} squares and there are {b} rows. How many squares are there in all the rows?
Answer: {r}.

explain.perimeter: {w_perimeter} is the perimeter. The question is about the area.

M4.rect-sides.03.text: The side of a square is {a} cm. Find its perimeter.
solution: The perimeter is all the sides added together, and a square has four sides of {a} cm.
Adding equal numbers is multiplying: {a} × {=4} = {r}.

Each side is {a} cm and there are four sides. How can you add {a} four times more quickly?

M4.rect-sides.04.text: The perimeter of a rectangle is {x} cm and one side is {a} cm. Find the other side.

One length and one width together: {x} : {=2} = {=x/2} cm.

M4.rect-sides.05.text: The floor of a room is a rectangle, {a} m by {b} m. How many square metres is the floor?

One row holds {a} such squares and there are {b} rows.
Area of the floor: {a} × {b} = {r} m².

One row holds {a} squares and there are {b} rows. How many squares are there in all?

M4.rect-sides.06.text: A plot is a rectangle, {a} m by {b} m. How long a fence is needed all the way round the plot?

Two sides are {a} m and two are {b} m. Add {a} + {b} and think how many such pairs you need.

M4.rect-sides.07.text: Rectangle A is {a} cm by {b} cm. Rectangle B is {c} cm by {d} cm. Compare the perimeters of A and B. Which sign goes between them?

Perimeter of B: {=2} × ({c} + {d}) = {=2*(c+d)} cm.

explain.widths-compared: The sign {w_widths_compared} comes from comparing only the widths {b} and {d}. The perimeter uses both sides: compare {=a+b} and {=c+d}.

M4.rect-sides.08.text: The sides of a rectangle are {a} m and {b} dm. Find its area in square decimetres.

There are {=10} dm in one metre, so {a} m = {a} × {=10} = {=10*a} dm.

Change {a} m to decimetres: {a} × {=10} = {=10*a}. Then multiply by the other side.

M4.rect-sides.09.text: The area of a rectangle is {x} cm² and one side is {a} cm. Find the other side.

So we find the unknown side by dividing the area by the known side.
The other side: {x} : {a} = {r} cm.

M4.rect-sides.10.text: There are two rooms: {a} m by {b} m and {c} m by {d} m. What is their total area in square metres?

First room: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. Now find the second room and add.

M4.rect-sides.11.text: A floor measuring {x} m by {y} m is to be covered with square tiles with sides of {=2} m. How many tiles are needed?

Along the side of {y} m there is room for {y} : {=2} = {b|tile|tiles|tiles}.

Along {x} m there fit {x} : {=2} = {a} tiles. Do the same for the other side, then multiply.

M4.not-rect.01.text: A shape is made of two rectangles that do not overlap: {a} by {b} and {c} by {d}. Find the area of the shape.

The parts do not overlap, so we add the areas: {=a*b} + {=c*d} = {r}.

First rectangle: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. Find the second one and add them.

M4.not-rect.02.text: A rectangle of {c} by {d} is cut out of the corner of a rectangle of {a} by {b}. Find the area of the shape that is left.

The part that was cut out: {c} × {d} = {=c*d}; it is no longer in the shape.
Subtract: {=a*b} − {=c*d} = {r}.

The whole rectangle: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. Now find the area of the corner that was cut out, {c} by {d}, and take it away.
Answer: {r}.

M4.not-rect.03.text: A rectangle of {c} by {d} is cut out of the corner of a rectangle of {a} by {b}. Find the perimeter of the shape that is left.

Pieces of two sides are gone, but two sides of the cut-out appeared, and together they are just as long. What is the perimeter of the whole {a} by {b} rectangle?

M4.not-rect.04.text: A frame: the outer rectangle is {a} by {b} and the inner rectangle is {c} by {d}. Find the area of the frame.

Area of the inner, empty one: {c} × {d} = {=c*d}.

M4.not-rect.05.text: A cross is made of five squares with sides of {a} cm. Find its perimeter in centimetres.

M4.not-rect.06.text: A shape is made of three rectangles: {a} by {b}, {c} by {d} and {e} by {f}. Find the area of the shape.
solution: Area of the first rectangle: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}.
Area of the second: {c} × {d} = {=c*d}.
Area of the third: {e} × {f} = {=e*f}.
Add all three: {=a*b} + {=c*d} + {=e*f} = {r}.

First: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}, second: {c} × {d} = {=c*d}. Find the third and add all three.
Answer: {r}.

explain.perimeters-added: {w_perimeters_added} is the sum of the perimeters of the three rectangles. The question is about the sum of their areas: {=a*b} + {=c*d} + {=e*f}.

M4.not-rect.07.text: A staircase is made of squares with sides of {a} cm: the bottom row has {b|square|squares|squares}, the row above has one square fewer, and so on up to one square at the top. Find the perimeter of the staircase in centimetres.
solution: Slide the steps towards the sides of the big square: the outline does not get shorter or longer.
The side of the big square is {b|square|squares|squares} of {a} cm, that is {b} × {a} = {=a*b} cm.
Perimeter: {=a*b} × {=4} = {r} cm.

The side of the big square is {b} × {a} = {=a*b} cm. What is its perimeter?
Answer: {r}.

explain.area: {w_area} is the area of the staircase. The question is about the perimeter.
explain.two-sides: {w_two_sides} is {=a*b} + {=a*b}: the left and the bottom sides. The stepped side is just as long: {=2*a*b} + {=2*a*b} = {r}.
explain.all-squares: {w_all_squares} is the perimeters of all the small squares added together. The sides shared inside are not part of the perimeter.

M4.not-rect.08.text: A plot of {a} m by {b} m has a path {c} m wide all the way round it. Find the area of the path.
solution: The path is on both sides, so the length and width with the path are bigger by {c} + {c} = {=2*c} m.
Plot with path: {=a+2*c} × {=b+2*c} = {=(a+2*c)*(b+2*c)} m².
Plot without path: {a} × {b} = {=a*b} m², and the path is the difference: {=(a+2*c)*(b+2*c)} − {=a*b} = {r} m².
hints: The plot together with the path makes a bigger rectangle. What are its sides?
{c} m is added on each side, so it is {=a+2*c} by {=b+2*c}. Find its area and subtract the area of the plot.
Answer: {r}.

explain.path-on-one-side: {w_path_on_one_side} comes from putting the path on only two sides, but it goes all the way round the plot.

M4.not-rect.09.text: A shape made of two rectangles has an area of {x}. The first rectangle is {a} by {b} and one side of the second is {c}. Find the other side of the second rectangle.
solution: Area of the first rectangle: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}.
What is left for the second: {x} − {=a*b} = {=x-a*b}.
The area of the second is {c} times the unknown side, so we divide: {=x-a*b} : {c} = {r}.
hints: The shape is made of two rectangles. How much of the area does the first one take?
First: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. How much area is left for the second one, if the whole shape is {x}?
Answer: {r}.

explain.area-of-the-second: {w_area_of_the_second} is the area of the second rectangle. The question is about its side.

explain.second-minus-side: {w_second_minus_side} comes from taking the side {c} away from the area of the second rectangle {=c*d}. A side is found by dividing: {=c*d} : {c}.

M4.not-rect.10.text: A square with a side of {c} is cut out of a rectangle of {a} by {b}. Find the area of the shape that is left.
solution: Area of the rectangle: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}.
Area of the square that was cut out: {c} × {c} = {=c*c}.
Subtract what was cut out: {=a*b} − {=c*c} = {r}.

Rectangle: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. Find the area of the square with a side of {c} and subtract it.
Answer: {r}.

explain.added: {w_added} comes from adding. The part that was cut out must be taken away.
explain.cut-part: {w_cut_part} is the area of the square {c} by {c} that was cut out. The question is about what is left: {=a*b} − {=c*c}.

M4.not-rect.11.text: A square with a side of {a} cm and a square with a side of {b} cm are put together so that the whole side of the smaller one touches the larger one. Find the perimeter of the shape.
solution: Perimeter of the big square: {a} × {=4} = {=4*a}; of the small one: {b} × {=4} = {=4*b}.
The common side of length {b} is now inside the shape. We take it away from both squares: {b} + {b} = {=2*b}.
Perimeter: {=4*a} + {=4*b} − {=2*b} = {r} cm.
hints: The common side is inside the shape, so it is not part of the border.
The perimeters are {=4*a} and {=4*b}. The common side of {b} is hidden in both squares. How much must you take away?
Answer: {r}.

explain.perimeters-added: {w_perimeters_added} is the two perimeters added together. The common side is inside the shape and is not part of the perimeter.

explain.area: {w_area} is the sum of the areas of the two squares. The question is about the perimeter, the length of the border.

M4.side-from-perimeter.01.text: The perimeter of a square is {x} cm. Find its side.
solution: A square has four equal sides, and together they make {x} cm.
Share equally: {x} : {=4} = {r} cm.

Divide {x} by {=4}: that gives the length of one side.
Answer: {r}.

explain.half: {w_half} is half the perimeter, but a square has four sides.
explain.perimeter-itself: {w_perimeter_itself} is the perimeter {x}. The side of a square is the perimeter divided by {=4}.
explain.divided-by-three: {w_divided_by_three} comes from dividing by {=3}, as for a triangle. A square has four sides: {x} : {=4}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.02.text: The perimeter of a rectangle is {a} m and one side is {b} cm. Find the other side in centimetres.
solution: {a} × {=100} = {=a*100}. The perimeter is {=a*100} cm, because there are {=100} cm in a metre.
{=a*100} : {=2} = {=a*50}. Two neighbouring sides together make this many centimetres.
hints: The sides are in different units. Change the perimeter to centimetres first.
The perimeter is {=a*100} cm. Half of it is one length and one width together. How much is left after the known side of {b} cm is taken away?
Answer: {r}.

explain.not-halved: {w_not_halved} comes from taking the side away from the whole perimeter. First halve the perimeter to get {=a*50}, and only then take away {b}: {r}.
explain.side-doubled-forgotten: {w_side_doubled_forgotten} comes from taking the side {b} away from the perimeter once and then halving. The perimeter has two sides of {b}: {=a*100} − {=2*b} = {=a*100-2*b}, those are the two other sides together, and one of them is {r}.
explain.two-sides-left: {w_two_sides_left} is {=a*100} − {=2*b}: the two sides of {b} are taken away and the two other sides together are left. We want one side, so we divide by {=2}: {r}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.03.text: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is {x} cm. Find its side.
solution: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides, and together they make {x} cm.

explain.divided-by-four: {w_divided_by_four} comes from dividing by {=4}, as for a square. A triangle has three sides: {x} : {=3}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.04.text: The perimeter of a regular pentagon is {x} cm. Find its side.
solution: A regular pentagon has five equal sides, and together they make {x} cm.

explain.perimeter-itself: {w_perimeter_itself} is the perimeter. The side is five times smaller.
explain.divided-by-four: {w_divided_by_four} comes from dividing by {=4}, as for a square. A pentagon has five sides: {x} : {=5}.
explain.divided-by-six: {w_divided_by_six} comes from dividing by {=6}, as for a hexagon. A pentagon has five sides: {x} : {=5}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.05.text: The length of a rectangle is twice its width and the perimeter is {x} cm. Find the width.
solution: The length is two widths. Go round the outline: length, width, length, width.
Altogether the perimeter holds {=2} + {=1} + {=2} + {=1} = {=6} widths.
One width: {x} : {=6} = {r} cm.

Go round: length (two widths), width, length (two widths), width. How many widths is that in all?

explain.divided-by-four: {w_divided_by_four} comes from dividing by {=4}, as for a square. A rectangle has two lengths and two widths, and a length is two widths: six widths in all, {x} : {=6}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.06.text: The perimeter of a regular hexagon is {x} cm. Find its side.
solution: A regular hexagon has six equal sides, and together they make {x} cm.

Divide {x} by {=6}: that gives the length of one side.

explain.perimeter-itself: {w_perimeter_itself} is the perimeter. The side is six times smaller.

explain.divided-by-five: {w_divided_by_five} comes from dividing by {=5}, as for a pentagon. A hexagon has six sides: {x} : {=6}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.07.text: The perimeter of an isosceles triangle is {x} cm and each of the two equal sides is {a} cm. Find the base.
solution: The two equal sides of an isosceles triangle together make {a} + {a} = {=2*a} cm.

Take {=2*a} away from the perimeter {x}. What is left is the base.

explain.one-leg-subtracted: {w_one_leg_subtracted} comes from taking away only one equal side. There are two of them.
explain.divided-by-three: {w_divided_by_three} comes from dividing the perimeter {x} by {=3}, as for an equilateral triangle. The sides here are not all equal: you take away the two equal sides.
explain.half-minus-leg: {w_half_minus_leg} comes from the way you find a side of a rectangle: half the perimeter minus a side. In a triangle you take the two equal sides of {a} away from the perimeter: {x} − {=2*a}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.08.text: The perimeter of a square is {x} cm. Find its area.
solution: First the side: four equal sides make {x} cm, so {x} : {=4} = {b} cm.
The area of a square is the side times itself: {b} × {b} = {r} cm².

The side is {x} : {=4} = {b}. How do you find the area of a square from its side?

explain.side-only: {w_side_only} is the side. The question is about the area.

M4.side-from-perimeter.09.text: The perimeter of a rectangle is {x} cm and one side is {a} cm. Find the area.
solution: Length and width together are half the perimeter: {x} : {=2} = {=x/2} cm.
The other side: {=x/2} − {a} = {=x/2-a} cm.
Area: {a} × {=x/2-a} = {r} cm².
hints: You need both sides to find the area. Find the other side first.
Half the perimeter is {=x/2}. Take away {a} to get the other side, then multiply the two sides.

explain.half-perimeter-times-side: {w_half_perimeter_times_side} comes from multiplying half the perimeter by the side. You need the second side for that: {=x/2} − {a}.
explain.perimeter-times-side: {w_perimeter_times_side} is the perimeter {x} times the side {a}. The area is the product of the two sides, and the second side is found as {=x/2} − {a}.
explain.other-side: {w_other_side} is the second side: one step short of the area. Now multiply it by the side {a}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.10.text: The perimeter of a regular octagon is {x} cm. Find its side.
solution: A regular octagon has eight equal sides, and together they make {x} cm.

explain.perimeter-itself: {w_perimeter_itself} is the perimeter. The side is eight times smaller.

explain.divided-by-four: {w_divided_by_four} comes from dividing by {=4}, as for a square. An octagon has eight sides: {x} : {=8}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.11.text: The sides of a rectangle are in the ratio {=2} : {=3} and the perimeter is {x} cm. Find the longer side.

One part: {x} : {=10} = {b} cm, and the longer side is {b} × {=3} = {r} cm.

The outline has {=10} equal parts. How long is one part, if the perimeter is {x} cm?
Answer: {r}.

explain.shorter: {w_shorter} is the shorter side. The question is about the longer one.

M4.same-area.01.text: A rectangle has sides {a} and {x}. Another rectangle with the same area has a side of {y}. Find its other side.
solution: Area of the first rectangle: {a} × {x} = {=a*x}.
The second rectangle has the same area, and one of its sides is {y}.
The other side: {=a*x} : {y} = {r}.
hints: Find the area of the first rectangle: multiply its sides.
The area is {=a*x}. The second rectangle has the same area and one side of {y}. How do you find the other side?
Answer: {r}.

explain.first-side: {w_first_side} is a side of the first rectangle. The other rectangle has different sides.

explain.second-side: {w_second_side} is the second side of the first rectangle. The areas are the same, but the sides are different: {=a*x} : {y}.

M4.same-area.02.text: The area of a rectangle is {x} cm² and one side is {a} cm. Find the perimeter.
solution: The other side: {x} : {a} = {=x/a} cm, because the area is the product of the sides.
Two neighbouring sides together: {a} + {=x/a} = {=a+x/a} cm.
The perimeter is two such sums: {=a+x/a} × {=2} = {r} cm.

The other side is {x} : {a} = {b}. Add two neighbouring sides, then double the sum.
Answer: {r}.

explain.half-perimeter: {w_half_perimeter} is the sum of the two sides {a} and {b}. The perimeter is all four sides, so the sum is doubled.

M4.same-area.03.text: A rectangle with sides {m} and {n} and a rectangle with sides {k} and {l} have the same area. Compare the perimeters of the first and the second. Which sign goes between them?
solution: The areas are equal: {m} × {n} = {=m*n} and {k} × {l} = {=k*l}.
Perimeter of the first: {=2} × ({m} + {n}) = {=2*(m+n)}. Perimeter of the second: {=2} × ({k} + {l}) = {=2*(k+l)}.
Compare {=2*(m+n)} and {=2*(k+l)}: the sign between the perimeters is {r}.
hints: The areas are equal, but each perimeter must be found on its own.
First: {=2} × ({m} + {n}) = {=2*(m+n)}. Find the perimeter of the second and compare.
Answer: {r}.

explain.equal: The sign = would be right if the perimeters were equal. With the same area the perimeters are not always equal: the closer the sides are to each other, the smaller the perimeter.
explain.reversed: The sign {w_reversed} comes from thinking that the longer, thinner rectangle has the smaller perimeter. With the same area, the perimeter is smaller for the rectangle whose sides are closer to each other.

M4.same-area.04.text: How many different rectangles with whole sides have an area of {a}? Rectangles with sides {=2} and {=3} and with sides {=3} and {=2} count as the same.
solution: The sides of the rectangle multiply to {a}.
These pairs of sides fit: {pairs}.
A pair in the other order is the same rectangle, so each is counted once.
So the number of rectangles is {r}.
hints: Write down all the divisors of {a}.
Put the divisors into pairs that multiply to {a}. A pair in the other order is the same rectangle.
Answer: {r}.

explain.ordered-pairs: {w_ordered_pairs} counts pairs more than once: a rectangle {=2} by {=3} and one {=3} by {=2} are the same.

explain.without-the-strip: {w_without_the_strip} is the count without the thinnest rectangle, {=1} by {a}. It fits as well: its sides are whole numbers.

M4.same-area.05.text: A rectangle with sides {x} and {b} and a square have the same area. Find the side of the square.
solution: Area of the rectangle: {x} × {b} = {y}.
The area of a square is its side times itself, so we look for the number that gives {y} when multiplied by itself.
That is {r}, because {r} × {r} = {y}. The side of the square is {r}.
hints: Find the area of the rectangle: the square has the same area.
The area is {y}. Which number multiplied by itself gives {y}?
Answer: {r}.

explain.longer-side: {w_longer_side} is the longer side of the rectangle, but the side of the square is smaller.

explain.mean-of-sides: {w_mean_of_sides} is the mean of the two sides of the rectangle. The side of a square with the same area is the number that gives {y} when multiplied by itself.

M4.same-area.06.text: The area of a rectangle is {x}. The length is doubled and the width is halved. What is the area now?
solution: If one side is multiplied by {=2} and the other is divided by {=2}, one change cancels the other.
The area has not changed: {x} × {=2} : {=2} = {r}.
hints: What happens to the area when one side is doubled?
And when the other side is halved? Think how the two changes work together on the area {x}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.doubled: {w_doubled} comes from doubling the area, but the other side was made half as long.

explain.perimeter-like: {w_perimeter_like} is the sum of the sides times {=2}. The question is about the area, and it did not change.

M4.same-area.07.text: A rectangle {x} by {y} is cut into pieces and the pieces are put together to make a square, with no gaps and no overlaps. Find the side of the square.

{=x*y} : {r} = {r}. Check: a square with a side of {r} has an area of {r} × {r} = {=x*y}.
So the side of the square is {r}.
hints: The area does not change when the pieces are moved. Find the area of the rectangle.
The area is {=x*y}. Which number multiplied by itself gives {=x*y}?
Answer: {r}.

explain.mean-of-sides: {w_mean_of_sides} is the mean of the two sides of the rectangle. A square with a side of {w_mean_of_sides} would have a different area. The side of the square is found from the area {=x*y}: {r} × {r} = {=x*y}.
explain.area-over-four: {w_area_over_four} comes from dividing the area by {=4}. That is how you find a side from a perimeter. Here the area is known, so look for the number that gives {=x*y} when multiplied by itself: {r}.

M4.same-area.08.text: The area of a rectangle with whole sides is {a}. What is the smallest perimeter it can have?

Their perimeters: {e2}.
{e3}. This is the smallest perimeter: it belongs to the rectangle whose sides are closest to each other.

Which rectangle has sides closest to each other? Find its perimeter.
Answer: {r}.

M4.same-area.09.text: The area of a rectangle with whole sides is {a}. What is the largest perimeter it can have?
solution: The longer and thinner the rectangle, the bigger its perimeter; the thinnest has a side of {=1}.
Then the other side is {a} : {=1} = {a}.

Take the sides {=1} and {a}. Find the perimeter of that rectangle.
Answer: {r}.

explain.half: {w_half} is half the perimeter, but the perimeter is twice as much.

explain.forgot-width: {w_forgot_width} is {a} + {a}, two lengths. The rectangle {=1} by {a} also has two widths of {=1}: {=2*a} + {=2} = {r}.

M4.same-area.10.text: A rectangle with sides {x} and {b} and a square with a side of {y} have the same area. By how much is the perimeter of the rectangle bigger than the perimeter of the square?

Perimeter of the square: {=4} × {y} = {=4*y}.
Difference: {=2*(x+b)} − {=4*y} = {r}.

Rectangle: {=2} × ({x} + {b}) = {=2*(x+b)}. Find the perimeter of the square with a side of {y} and subtract.
Answer: {r}.

M4.same-area.11.text: One side of a rectangle {a} by {b} is doubled and the other is tripled. What is the area of the new rectangle?

M5.grid.01.text: A shape on squared paper is made of {a} whole squares and {b|half square|half squares|half squares}. The side of one square is {=1} cm. Find the area in square centimetres.

{b} halves make {=b/2} whole squares. Add them to the whole squares you already have.

M5.grid.02.text: A right-angled triangle on squared paper has legs of {a} and {b|square|squares|squares}. The side of one square is {=1} cm. Find the area in square centimetres.

explain.rectangle: {w_rectangle} is the area of the rectangle {a} by {b}, and the triangle is half of it: {a} × {b} : {=2} = {r}.

M5.grid.03.text: A shape on squared paper is made of {a|row|rows|rows} of {b|square|squares|squares}. The side of one square is {=1} cm. Find the area in square centimetres.

Answer: {r}.

Next rows: {c} × {d} = {=c*d} squares.

First part: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. Find the second part and add.

explain.one-joint-too-many: {w_one_joint_too_many} comes from counting {a} shared sides. The first square has no square before it, so there are {=a-1}: {=4*a} − {=a-1} × {=2} = {r}.

M4.rect-squares.13.text: A square of {c} by {c} is cut out of the middle of a rectangle of {a} by {b|square|squares|squares}, without touching the edges. The side of one square is {=1} cm. Find the perimeter of the figure in centimetres: count the outer edge and the edge of the hole.
solution: {=2} × ({a} + {b}) = {=2*(a+b)}. This is the outer edge of the figure.
{c} × {=4} = {=4*c}. This is the edge of the hole: a square has four sides of {c} cm.
hints: The figure has two edges: the outer one and the edge of the hole. Find both.
Outer edge: {=2} × ({a} + {b}) = {=2*(a+b)}. Now find the edge of the hole, a square of {c} by {c}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.outer-only: {w_outer_only} is only the outer edge. The edge of the hole is part of the perimeter too: {=2*(a+b)} + {=4*c} = {r}.
explain.hole-area-added: {w_hole_area_added} comes from adding the number of squares in the hole to the outer edge. What you add is the length of the edge of the hole: {c} × {=4} = {=4*c}, so {r}.
explain.one-side-of-hole: {w_one_side_of_hole} comes from adding only one side of the hole, {c}. The hole is a square with four sides: {c} × {=4} = {=4*c}, so {r}.

M4.rect-squares.14.text: A frame one square wide is laid round a rectangle of {a} by {b|square|squares|squares}. How many squares are in the frame?
solution: The frame and the rectangle together make a bigger rectangle, {=a+2} by {=b+2}: one square is added on every side.
{=a+2} × {=b+2} = {=(a+2)*(b+2)} squares in the big rectangle.
Take away the inner ones: {=(a+2)*(b+2)} − {a} × {b} = {r}.
hints: The frame and the rectangle together form a bigger rectangle. What size is it?
One square is added on every side, so it is {=a+2} by {=b+2}. Find the squares of the big rectangle and take away the inner ones.
Answer: {r}.

explain.without-corners: {w_without_corners} is {=2} × ({a} + {b}), the squares along the sides. The four corner squares of the frame count too: {w_without_corners} + {=4} = {r}.
explain.whole-figure: {w_whole_figure} is the number of squares in the rectangle and the frame together. The rectangle inside already has {a} × {b} = {=a*b} squares, and those are taken away: {r}.
explain.two-corners: {w_two_corners} is {=2} × ({a} + {b}) with only two corners added. The frame has four corner squares: {=2*(a+b)} + {=4} = {r}.

M4.rect-sides.12.text: A room is a rectangle, {a} m by {b} m. A skirting board is needed along all the walls except the door, which is {c|metre|metres|metres} wide. How many metres of skirting board are needed?
solution: {=2} × ({a} + {b}) = {=2*(a+b)}. This is the perimeter of the room, the length of all the walls.
{=2*(a+b)} − {c} = {r}. No skirting board is needed along the door.
So {r|metre|metres|metres} of skirting board are needed.
hints: Find the length of all the walls together, the perimeter.
The perimeter is {=2*(a+b)} m. What do you do about the door, which is {c|metre|metres|metres} wide?
Answer: {r}.

explain.door-ignored: {w_door_ignored} is the length of all the walls. There is no skirting board along the door, so its width is taken away: {=2*(a+b)} − {c} = {r}.
explain.door-twice: {w_door_twice} comes from taking the width of the door away twice. There is one door, so its width is taken away once: {=2*(a+b)} − {c} = {r}.
explain.door-added: {w_door_added} comes from adding the width of the door. The door is a gap in the skirting board, so its width is taken away: {=2*(a+b)} − {c} = {r}.

M4.rect-sides.13.text: The sides of a rectangle are {a} m and {b} cm. Find its perimeter in centimetres.
solution: {a} × {=100} = {=a*100}. That is how many centimetres there are in {a} m.
{=a*100} + {b} = {=a*100+b}. This is the sum of two neighbouring sides.
hints: The sides are in different units. Change the metres to centimetres first.
{a} m is {=a*100} cm. Add the other side, then think how many such pairs the perimeter has.
Answer: {r}.

explain.units-added: {w_units_added} comes from adding numbers in different units, {a} + {b}. Change the metres to centimetres first: {a} × {=100} = {=a*100}, and the perimeter is {r}.
explain.metre-as-ten: {w_metre_as_ten} comes from counting {=10} centimetres in a metre. There are {=100} centimetres in a metre: ({a} × {=100} + {b}) × {=2} = {r}.
explain.half-perimeter: {w_half_perimeter} is the sum of two neighbouring sides. The perimeter is twice as much: {=a*100+b} × {=2} = {r}.

M4.rect-sides.14.text: A rectangular pen has one side against a wall, and no fence is needed on that side. The pen is {b} m long along the wall and {a} m wide. How many metres of fence are needed?
solution: Fence is needed on three sides: one side of {b} m and two sides of {a} m.
So {r|metre|metres|metres} of fence are needed.
hints: Fence is not needed on all the sides. On which sides is it?
There is no fence along the wall. What is left is one side of {b} m and two more sides. How long are those two?
Answer: {r}.

explain.full-perimeter: {w_full_perimeter} is the perimeter of the pen. No fence is needed on the side by the wall: {b} + {a} + {a} = {r}.
explain.one-width-only: {w_one_width_only} comes from counting the width only once. The pen has two short sides of {a} m: {b} + {a} + {a} = {r}.
explain.wall-side-swapped: {w_wall_side_swapped} comes from fencing two sides of {b} m and only one of {a} m. The wall is along a side of {b} m, so that side needs no fence: {b} + {a} + {a} = {r}.

M4.rect-sides.15.text: A rectangle {a} by {b} is cut into two parts by one straight cut of length {b}. By how much is the sum of the perimeters of the two parts bigger than the perimeter of the original rectangle?
solution: The cut runs inside the rectangle, and each of the two parts gets a new side of length {b}.
{b} × {=2} = {r}. The new sides are added to the sum of the perimeters of the two parts.
So the sum of the perimeters is bigger by {r}.
hints: Which new sides appear after the cut?
The cut of {b} is a side of both parts. How many times does it count in the sum of the two perimeters?
Answer: {r}.

explain.no-change: {w_no_change} comes from thinking that the cut changes nothing. The cut becomes a side of both parts, so {b} × {=2} = {r} is added.
explain.cut-once: {w_cut_once} comes from counting the cut once. It is a side of each of the two parts, so it counts twice: {b} × {=2} = {r}.
explain.sum-of-parts: {w_sum_of_parts} is {=2*a} + {=4*b}, the sum of the perimeters of the two parts. The question is how much bigger that is than the perimeter of the rectangle: {=2*a+4*b} − {=2*(a+b)} = {r}.

M4.not-rect.12.text: An L-shaped path runs along two neighbouring sides of a plot of {a} m by {b} m. The path is {c|metre|metres|metres} wide. Find the area of the path in square metres.
solution: Split the path into two rectangles: {a} by {c} and {c} by {=b-c}, so that the corner square is not counted twice.
So the area of the path is {r} m².
hints: Split the path into two rectangles so that the corner square is in only one of them.
One rectangle is {a} by {c}. How long is the second one if the corner square is taken out of its length?
Answer: {r}.

explain.corner-twice: {w_corner_twice} comes from counting the corner square twice: {a} × {c} + {b} × {c}. Its area is in both strips, so the second strip is made shorter by {c}: {a} × {c} + {c} × {=b-c} = {r}.
explain.rest-of-the-plot: {w_rest_of_the_plot} is the area of the plot without the path, but the question is about the path: {a} × {c} + {c} × {=b-c} = {r}.
explain.corner-removed-twice: {w_corner_removed_twice} comes from taking the corner square out of both strips. It must be taken out of only one: {a} × {c} + {c} × {=b-c} = {r}.

M4.not-rect.13.text: A rectangular garden is {a} m by {b} m. Two paths {c|metre|metres|metres} wide cross at a right angle: one runs along the garden and the other across it, both from edge to edge. Find the area of the garden without the paths, in square metres.
solution: Slide the paths to the edges of the garden: the area without paths does not change.
What is left is a rectangle {=a-c} by {=b-c}.
hints: What happens if you slide the paths to the edges of the garden? The area without paths stays the same.
{c} is taken from the length {a} and {c} from the width {b}. What are the sides of what is left?
Answer: {r}.

explain.crossing-counted-twice: {w_crossing_counted_twice} comes from taking both whole paths away from the area of the garden. The crossing {c} by {c} is in both paths, but it must be taken away only once. Correct: {=a-c} × {=b-c} = {r}.
explain.one-path-only: {w_one_path_only} is the garden without one path. The second path must be taken away too: {=a-c} × {=b-c} = {r}.
explain.paths-area: {w_paths_area} is the area of the paths themselves. The question is about the garden without them: {=a-c} × {=b-c} = {r}.

M4.not-rect.14.text: A rectangular notch {c} wide and {d} deep is cut into the side of length {a} of a rectangle of {a} by {b}. The ends of that side are left whole. Find the perimeter of the shape.
solution: {=2} × ({a} + {b}) = {=2*(a+b)}. This is the perimeter of the rectangle without the notch.
The notch takes away a piece of the side {c} wide, but adds a bottom of the same width. Two side walls of depth {d} are also added: {d} × {=2} = {=2*d}.
hints: Think about what the notch took away from the perimeter and what it added.
The bottom of the notch, {c} wide, replaces the piece of the side that was taken away. What else was added: how many walls, and how deep?
Answer: {r}.

explain.perimeter-unchanged: {w_perimeter_unchanged} comes from thinking that the perimeter stays the same, as when a corner is cut out. A notch in the middle of a side adds two walls of depth {d}: {=2*(a+b)} + {=2*d} = {r}.
explain.depth-once: {w_depth_once} comes from counting the depth of the notch once. A notch has two side walls of depth {d}: {=2*(a+b)} + {d} × {=2} = {r}.
explain.bottom-added: {w_bottom_added} comes from adding the bottom of the notch without taking away the piece of the side it replaces. Both are {c} wide and cancel each other: {=2*(a+b)} + {=2*d} = {r}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.12.text: The perimeter of a rectangle is {x} cm, and one side is {b} cm longer than the other. Find the shorter side.
solution: {x} : {=2} = {=x/2}. That is the length and the width together.
{=x/2} − {b} = {=x/2-b}. If the length were as short as the width, the two widths would make this much.
hints: First find the length and the width together.
Take the difference {b} away from {=x/2}. What is left is two of the shorter sides. How long is one?
Answer: {r}.

explain.longer-side: {w_longer_side} is the longer side, but the question is about the shorter one: {r}.
explain.difference-not-halved: {w_difference_not_halved} is {=x/2} − {b}, two shorter sides together. We want one, so we divide by {=2}: {r}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.13.text: How many different rectangles with whole sides in centimetres have a perimeter of {a} cm? Rectangles {=2} by {=3} and {=3} by {=2} count as the same, and a square is also a rectangle.
solution: {a} : {=2} = {=a/2}. Two neighbouring sides add up to {=a/2} cm.
The pairs of sides that fit: {e}.
{s} = {r}. Each pair is one rectangle.
hints: What is the sum of two neighbouring sides?
Write down the pairs of whole numbers with that sum, without repeating a pair in a different order.
Answer: {r}.

explain.ordered-pairs: {w_ordered_pairs} counts pairs more than once: {=1} + {=a/2-1} and {=a/2-1} + {=1} are the same rectangle. The same rectangles are counted once: {r}.
explain.square-left-out: {w_square_left_out} is the count without the square. A square is a rectangle too: its side is {=a/4}. Altogether {r}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.14.text: A rectangle is made of {a} identical squares in one row. The perimeter of the rectangle is {x} cm. Find the side of one square.
solution: The length of the rectangle is {a|side|sides|sides} of a square and the width is one side. The perimeter holds {a} + {=1} + {a} + {=1} = {=2*a+2|side|sides|sides} of a square.
So the side of one square is {r} cm.
hints: How many sides of a square does the perimeter of the rectangle hold?
The length is {a} sides and the width is one side, and each of them appears twice. Divide the perimeter by that number of sides.
Answer: {r}.

explain.half-perimeter-over-count: {w_half_perimeter_over_count} comes from dividing half the perimeter by the number of squares. Half the perimeter holds {a|side|sides|sides} of a square and one more, that is {=a+1|side|sides|sides}, so we divide by {=a+1}: {r}.
explain.not-halved: {w_not_halved} comes from dividing the whole perimeter by {=a+1}. The whole perimeter is {=2*a+2|side|sides|sides} of a square: {x} : {=2*a+2} = {r}.

M4.side-from-perimeter.15.text: A square with a side of {a} cm and a rectangle have the same perimeter. One side of the rectangle is {b} cm. Find the other side of the rectangle.
solution: {a} × {=4} = {=4*a}. This is the perimeter of the square, and also of the rectangle.
{=4*a} : {=2} = {=2*a}. Two neighbouring sides of the rectangle make this much.
hints: Find the perimeter of the square: the rectangle has the same.
The perimeter is {=4*a}. Half of it is two neighbouring sides of the rectangle. Take away the known side {b}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.square-side-taken: {w_square_side_taken} comes from thinking the other side of the rectangle equals the side of the square. The perimeters are equal, not the sides: {=2*a} − {b} = {r}.
explain.half-perimeter-only: {w_half_perimeter_only} is half the perimeter, that is two neighbouring sides together. The known side {b} must be taken away: {=2*a} − {b} = {r}.

M4.same-area.12.text: The side of a square is made {=1} cm longer, and the area grows by {x} cm². Find the side of the original square.
solution: Two strips {=1} cm wide are added along two sides of the square, and one corner square {=1} by {=1} cm.
{x} − {=1} = {=x-1}. This many square centimetres belong to the two strips.
{=x-1} : {=2} = {r}. This is the length of each strip, that is, the side of the square.
hints: Think about which parts are added to the square when its side grows by {=1} cm.
The corner square gives {=1} cm², and the other {=x-1} cm² are two equal strips. How long is each strip?
Answer: {r}.

explain.increase-as-side: {w_increase_as_side} is the growth of the area, not the side. It is made of two strips and one corner square: ({x} − {=1}) : {=2} = {r}.
explain.not-halved: {w_not_halved} is the area of the two strips together. There is one strip along each side, so we divide by {=2}: {r}.
explain.corner-added: {w_corner_added} comes from adding the corner square instead of taking it away: ({x} + {=1}) : {=2}. The corner square is part of the growth, and it is taken away before dividing: ({x} − {=1}) : {=2} = {r}.

M4.same-area.13.text: One side of a square with a side of {a} cm is made {b} cm longer, and the neighbouring side is made {b} cm shorter. By how many square centimetres does the area get smaller?
solution: New rectangle: {=a+b} by {=a-b}, its area is {=a+b} × {=a-b} = {=(a+b)*(a-b)}.
{=a*a} − {=(a+b)*(a-b)} = {r}. This many square centimetres less.
The area got smaller by {r} cm²: that is {b} × {b}.
hints: Find the sides and the area of the new rectangle.
The sides are {a} + {b} = {=a+b} and {a} − {b} = {=a-b}. Find the area and take it away from the area of the square.
Answer: {r}.

explain.unchanged: {w_unchanged} comes from thinking that one piece is added and another taken away, so the area stays the same. The area changes: {=a*a} − {=(a+b)*(a-b)} = {r}.
explain.shift-taken: {w_shift_taken} is the shift of the sides, not the change of the area. The area got smaller by {b} × {b} = {r}.
explain.both-shifts: {w_both_shifts} is the two shifts added, {b} + {b}. The area changed in another way: {=a*a} − {=(a+b)*(a-b)} = {r}.

M4.same-area.14.text: A rectangle with sides {x} cm and {y} cm and a square have the same perimeter. By how many square centimetres is the area of the square bigger than the area of the rectangle?
solution: {x} + {y} = {=x+y}. The square has the same sum of two neighbouring sides, so its side is {=x+y} : {=2} = {a}.
{a} × {a} = {=a*a} is the area of the square. {x} × {y} = {=x*y} is the area of the rectangle.
hints: The square and the rectangle have the same perimeter, so the same sum of two neighbouring sides.
{x} + {y} = {=x+y}, so the side of the square is {=x+y} : {=2}. Find both areas and subtract.
Answer: {r}.

explain.equal-areas: {w_equal_areas} comes from thinking that equal perimeters mean equal areas. Each area is found on its own: {=a*a} − {=x*y} = {r}.
explain.side-difference: {w_side_difference} is the difference of the sides of the rectangle, {x} − {y}. The question is about areas: {=a*a} − {=x*y} = {r}.
explain.square-side: {w_square_side} is the side of the square. The question is by how much its area is bigger: {=a*a} − {=x*y} = {r}.

M5.grid.12.text: A shape covers {a} squares of squared paper. The side of one square is {=5} mm. Find the area of the shape in square centimetres.
solution: {=5} mm = {=5/10} cm. The side of a square is {=5/10} cm.
{=5/10} × {=5/10} = {=25/100}. This is how many square centimetres one square covers.
hints: How many centimetres is the side of a square?
Find the area of one square in cm², then multiply by the number of squares, {a}.
Answer: {r}.

explain.side-not-squared: {w_side_not_squared} comes from using the side {=5/10} cm as the area of a square. The area of a square is side times side: {=25/100}. {a} × {=25/100} = {r}.
explain.square-millimetres: {w_square_millimetres} is the area in square millimetres: one square holds {=25} mm². In square centimetres a square covers {=25/100}: {a} × {=25/100} = {r}.
explain.comma-misplaced: In {w_comma_misplaced} the comma is in another place. One square covers {=25/100} cm², not {=25/10}: {a} × {=25/100} = {r}.

M5.grid.13.text: A shape on squared paper is made of two rectangles, with sizes in squares: {a} by {b} and {c} by {d}. They overlap in part: the common part is a rectangle {e} by {f}. How many squares does the shape have?
solution: {a} × {b} = {=a*b} and {c} × {d} = {=c*d}: the squares in each rectangle.
The squares of the common part, {e} × {f} = {=e*f}, were counted twice; they must be counted once.
hints: How many squares does each rectangle have?
Some squares were counted twice: those of the common part, {e} by {f}. What must you do about them?
Answer: {r}.

explain.overlap-counted-twice: {w_overlap_counted_twice} is the squares of both rectangles added. The common squares were counted twice, there are {e} × {f} = {=e*f} of them, and one count is taken away: {=a*b} + {=c*d} − {=e*f} = {r}.
explain.overlap-removed-twice: {w_overlap_removed_twice} comes from taking the common part away twice. The common squares were counted twice in the sum, so only one count is taken away: {=a*b} + {=c*d} − {=e*f} = {r}.

M5.grid.14.text: A board of {a} by {b} squares is coloured like a chessboard: neighbouring squares alternate in colour and the corner squares are black. How many black squares are there on the board?
solution: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. This is how many squares the board has.
Black and white squares alternate, and the corner squares are black: when the number of squares is odd, there is one more black than white.
hints: How many squares does the board have altogether?
Are there as many black as white, or more black? A corner square is black.
Answer: {r}.

explain.rounded-down: {w_rounded_down} is half of the squares, rounded down. The corner squares are black, so with an odd number of squares there is one more black one: {e}.
explain.rows-halved-down: {w_rows_halved_down} comes from taking half of the squares in each row, rounded down. A row of odd length that starts with a black square has one more black than white: {e}.

M5.sides.12.text: A floor is a rectangle, {x} m by {y} m. Carpet is sold in rolls {a|metre|metres|metres} wide. The floor is covered with strips, each running along the side of {y} m. How many metres of carpet are needed?
solution: {x} : {a} = {b}. This many strips must be laid side by side.
{b} × {y} = {r}. Each strip is {y} m long.
So {r|metre|metres|metres} of carpet are needed.
hints: How many strips {a|metre|metres|metres} wide fit across the floor?
There are {b} strips, each {y} m long. Multiply the number of strips by the length of one.
Answer: {r}.

explain.area-instead: {w_area_instead} is the area of the floor in square metres, but the question is about the length of carpet in metres. There are {b} strips, each {y} m long: {b} × {y} = {r}.
explain.one-strip: {w_one_strip} is the length of one strip. The floor is wider than one strip, so {b|strip|strips|strips} are needed: {b} × {y} = {r}.

M5.sides.13.text: A wall of {a} m by {b} m is to be painted. One litre of paint covers {c|square metre|square metres|square metres}. Paint is sold in cans of {d|litre|litres|litres}. How many cans are needed?
solution: {a} × {b} = {=a*b}. This is the area of the wall in square metres.
{c} × {d} = {=c*d}. One can covers this many square metres.
{=floor(a*b/(c*d))} + {=1} = {r}. The wall uses {=floor(a*b/(c*d))} full cans, and the rest of the wall must be painted too, so one more can is needed.
hints: Find the area of the wall and the area one can covers.
The wall is {=a*b} m² and one can covers {=c*d} m². How many cans is that? What do you do about the part left over?
Answer: {r}.

explain.rounded-down: {w_rounded_down} is the number of full cans. The rest of the wall must be painted too, so you take one more can: {r}.
explain.litres-as-cans: {w_litres_as_cans} is the number of litres needed, but paint is sold in cans of {d|litre|litres|litres}. One can covers {=c*d}: {=a*b} : {=c*d} with a remainder, so you need {r}.

M5.sides.14.text: A floor of {a} m by {b} m is to be covered with square tiles with a side of {c} cm. How many tiles are needed?
solution: {a} × {=100} = {=a*100}. {=a*100} : {c} = {=a*100/c}: this many tiles along the side of {a} m.
{=b*100} : {c} = {=b*100/c}: this many tiles along the side of {b} m.
hints: Change the sides of the floor to centimetres.
How many tiles with a side of {c} cm fit along each side? Then multiply the two numbers.
Answer: {r}.

explain.side-as-area: {w_side_as_area} comes from dividing the area of the floor in square metres by the side of a tile in metres. A tile has an area, not a length: along the sides there are {=a*100/c} and {=b*100/c} tiles, {r} altogether.
explain.area-over-side: {w_area_over_side} comes from dividing the area of the floor in square centimetres by the side of a tile. You must divide by the area of a tile, or count the tiles along the sides: {=a*100/c} × {=b*100/c} = {r}.

M5.sides.15.text: A floor of {x} m by {y} m is to be tiled completely with identical square tiles, without cutting any. The tiles are the biggest possible. How many tiles are needed?

explain.rates-added: {w_rates_added} comes from treating both pipes as filling. One fills and the other lets out, so only {b} − {a} = {=b-a} parts an hour are added: {=a*b} : {=b-a} = {r}.
explain.times-subtracted: {w_times_subtracted} is the difference of the times, {b} − {a}. The time is found from the parts per hour: {=a*b} : {=b-a} = {r}.

M14.average-speed.13.text: The speed of a boat in still water is {a} km/h and the speed of the current is {b} km/h. The boat went {c} km with the current and came back. How many hours was it on the way?
solution: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. That is the speed with the current. {c} : {=a+b} = {=c/(a+b)} hours.
{a} − {b} = {=a-b}. That is the speed against the current. {c} : {=a-b} = {=c/(a-b)} hours.
hints: Going with the current the boat is faster, against the current it is slower. Work out the time for each direction separately.
The speed with the current is {a} + {b}, against the current {a} − {b}. Divide {c} km by each speed and add the times.
Answer: {r}.

explain.still-water-speed: {w_still_water_speed} comes from ignoring the current: {=2*c} : {a}. With the current the boat is faster and against it slower: {=c/(a+b)} + {=c/(a-b)} = {r}.
explain.one-way: {w_one_way} is the time with the current only. The boat also has to come back, and against the current it is slower: {=c/(a+b)} + {=c/(a-b)} = {r}.
explain.both-ways-slow: {w_both_ways_slow} comes from using the speed against the current both ways. With the current the boat is faster: {=c/(a+b)} + {=c/(a-b)} = {r}.
explain.both-ways-fast: {w_both_ways_fast} comes from using the speed with the current both ways. On the way back the boat goes against the current, which is slower: {=c/(a+b)} + {=c/(a-b)} = {r}.

M14.average-speed.14.text: One worker does a job in {a|hour|hours|hours}, another in {b|hour|hours|hours} and a third in {c|hour|hours|hours}. In how many hours do the three of them do it together?
solution: Let the whole job be {x|part|parts|parts}. The parts an hour: {x} : {a} = {xa}, {x} : {b} = {xb}, {x} : {c} = {xc}.
{xa} + {xb} + {xc} = {xs}. That many parts the three do together in an hour.
hints: Take a number of parts for the job that all three times divide.
Add the parts an hour of the three workers and find the time.
Answer: {r}.

explain.average-of-times: {w_average_of_times} is the mean time of one worker. With three workers the job goes much faster: {x} : {xs} = {r}.
explain.two-workers-only: {w_two_workers_only} comes from leaving out the third worker. He works too, and together they do {xs} parts an hour: {x} : {xs} = {r}.
explain.sum-of-times: {w_sum_of_times} is the sum of the three times. With three workers the job goes faster than for any one alone: {x} : {xs} = {r}.
